- **Item 138, the owner’s roadmap interview (2026-10-14): a shared codebook, physics collapse and radar.** During S1’s stage demo, before its review (item 139), the owner asked to “use shared codebook concepts for scripting actions like ‘flee’ and ‘capture beacon’ to simplify and reduce communication overhead”, and to “plan for the shared codebook to be built-in but reconfigurable by the user”. The owner also asked to “roadmap real-physics for collapse of voxels including physics-calculated damage to units hit by falling materials”, and to “roadmap radar with real physics”, adding: “we may want to use this game to test concepts of radar coverage with real doppler effect simulated. roadmap further to include simulations for passive radar concepts involving illuminator of opportunity passive radar implementation using overhead illuminator to sim the effects of our sun on earth.” The owner then answered four questions, each with options that stated their downsides. The engineering calls below were made under the owner’s standing instruction of 2026-09-14 and are open to the owner’s overrule. This item changes no code, no proto and no rules row. It amends spec section 16: the S2 row gains (3)’s support rule, the S3 row gains (1)’s codebook, and the S4 row gains (1)’s radio codes. From S3 it extends the v1 vocabulary that spec section 10 and AGENTS.md §11 list as exact, by one construct: the codebook entry. S3’s plan carries those contract edits. **(1) The shared codebook: both layers, one codebook (the recommended option).** The owner chose the option that read: “From S3 (authoring), named plays are usable as steps and handlers in a playbook. From S4 (radio), the same names become brevity codes: a received code fires a handler the seat itself sealed, so radio still carries data and never control.” The game ships a built-in codebook, and the player may edit it, add entries and remove them. *Downside:* the codebook’s format becomes a contract at S3, and S4 adds a signal meaning on top of it. **Engineering calls:** (a) *An entry is a typed macro, not a script.* An entry has a name, value-typed parameter slots and a body. The slots hold a place, a selector, a game time in ms, an amount in `$` or a count; a slot never holds a step, a handler or an entry. The body is a step sequence in v1 vocabulary, used where a route step or a handler body (`Handler.body`, `repeated Step`) stands. Labels inside a body are local and renamed on expansion, and no jump leaves the entry, so the halting argument for playbooks holds. In S3’s first cut, a body may not name another entry. That rules out cycles, needs no depth cap (which would otherwise need its own in-world reason), and keeps the codebook clear of AGENTS.md §2’s “mini-language of your own”. Nesting is revisited only on evidence. The entry holds no flag, branch or repeat, and fills none of the reserved script seams. If a reusable handler, `on_death` or `fallback` is wanted later, it is a separate kind at playbook level, with its own id handling. (b) *One expansion, in the sim.* The expansion is a pure function beside `Plan::compile` in `pharmakos-sim`, so the verifier, plan-core (which depends on the verifier, never the reverse), the gateway, `gamectl` and the compile all call the same code. It substitutes typed values into typed fields, never text into text. It is determinism code under AGENTS.md §5: a change to it re-blesses the chains it moves, and the plan fingerprint covers the playbook as sealed, including its carried entries. (c) *Bounded before it is built.* The codebook file and a playbook’s carried entries are untrusted input. Their decoder caps the entry count, the steps per body, the parameter slots and the name length. The expanded size is computed from the entries, with checked arithmetic, before any step is built, and the playbook is refused with a typed diagnostic once it passes the size budget. A property test holds that a crafted file only ever returns the typed error. (d) *A sealed playbook is self-contained.* It carries the entries it uses, so a seal, its `report_hash`, its fingerprint and its replay never depend on a codebook file on someone’s disk. The carried copy is what runs. A lint flags a carried entry nothing names, and another flags a carried copy that differs from the player’s codebook; neither is stripped silently. (e) *The size budget counts the expansion.* The budget bounds a decision tick’s cost (P1 measures nanoseconds per size unit per decision tick) and keeps FULL under its bound (spec section 10). An entry named ten times costs ten times, plus whatever item 94’s unit definition charges for the reference itself, which S3’s plan states. The saving is in what the player writes and reads, and from S4 in radio traffic, not in the budget. (f) *Diagnostics.* A diagnostic inside an entry carries the pointer into the carried entry and the pointers of the places that name it. Rows for the same fault are merged by the entry pointer. A Fix says whether it patches the naming place or the carried entry. This changes `gp.v1`’s diagnostic and `report_hash`’s inputs, a contract change in S3’s plan. (g) *Where it lives, and secrecy.* The built-in codebook ships as data the gateway reads, like `library/`, and the built-in operator reads only the built-in entries, so a player’s edits never change how the operator plays. A player’s edited codebook is that seat’s private data in the user data folder, like drafts. Only that seat’s token reads it: no other seat, no advisor token (`ADVISOR_METHODS` is unchanged) and no admin scope. A seat’s carried entries never leave the gateway for another seat. (h) *Radio codes, for S4’s plan.* A code goes on the air as a bounded id into the sending seat’s sealed code table, never as an entry’s text. Only a sealed `broadcast` step sends one; live player input never does (AGENTS.md §11, no manual control). A receiver acts only on its own seat’s codes, and a code it does not know is dropped and counted under a reason code. As built today, a go-code is a condition that an Attack launch, an on-site setting or a route step waits on; it never fires a handler (spec section 8; `GoCode` in `playbook.proto`). S4’s plan keeps that shape: a received code is a `Condition` predicate over the seat’s knowledge, under the handlers’ existing `cooldown_ms` and `max_fires` limits. Which party receives a code (the commander, a beacon in mast coverage, or both) is S4’s to state. A code that fires a handler directly would be a new radio receive path, widening the spoofing surface the spec keeps on the roadmap, so it is the owner’s risk call when S4 plans it. **(2) ‘Capture beacon’: the codebook now, capture later (the recommended option).** Capture stays on the roadmap. Section 2.2 decided destroy-only for v1, and capture objectives keep the proto numbers reserved for them (spec section 10; `playbook.proto`’s reserved `capture`). v1’s built-in codebook ships entries written in v1 vocabulary: among them flee (the `flee_to_safety` and `flee_wait` pair that `library/hold_and_build.jsonc` already carries), hold, regroup and fall back to the core. A `capture_beacon` entry arrives when capture leaves the roadmap. *Downside:* the owner’s own example entry waits until after v1. **(3) Physics collapse: after v1, with S2 building the seam (the recommended option).** The owner chose the option that read: “S2 ships a simple deterministic support rule (detached voxels fall, a flat damage rule) behind an interface that real physics replaces later. Physics collapse with impact damage (mass, velocity, kinetic energy in fixed point) goes on the roadmap after v1.” *Downside:* v1’s collapse looks simpler than the vision, and the later swap moves every hash chain, as a new rules version. The support rule’s constants are tuning rows, proposed in S2’s plan, or PLACEHOLDERs until then. Mine’s pillar spacing counts against the rule, which is what the setting was drafted for: section 3’s draft Mine is “keep a support pillar every N tiles”. S1’s plan noted that without a collapse rule, pillars only cost yield. **Engineering calls, for S2’s plan:** the support search is bounded and incremental, with its worst case (one crater cutting off a large region) measured in G3′, not only its mean. Its order is total: seeds sorted by voxel index, a breadth-first search, and clusters numbered by their lowest voxel, because which voxels land where is hashed behaviour. S2’s plan also states where collapse sits in the tick’s phase order, how it invalidates the HPA* cluster cache, and its allocations against `crates/sim/tests/allocations.rs`. A voxel reaches the chunk store only through `set` or `crater` (AGENTS.md §4.8). **Raised to the owner by S2’s plan,** because the spec does not state them (AGENTS.md §12): whether units, structures, beacons and the core standing on a falling region fall with it or take damage; who is credited with a kill by collapse that an enemy’s crater caused; and whether Mine’s tunnelling may collapse an enemy’s ground. **For the physics roadmap entry:** while it falls, a body is a hashed entity table under §4.8’s three places, leaving the chunks through `set` or `crater` and returning through `set` at rest. Its collision is swept, or stepped one voxel at a time, so a fast body cannot pass through a thin floor. Energy is computed in `i128` or a scaled unit, with a stated worst case: the map’s height bounds speed, and its volume bounds mass. Impacts apply in the order (tick, body id, unit id). Damage is capped at the HP left, as a stated rule, not a silent clamp. The damage covers units, as the owner asked, and structures, for consistency. **(4) Radar: not decided; prepare for two paths.** The owner answered: “great question.  im not sure yet on the details.  prepare for #1 or #3”. The paths are the question’s options 1 and 3. *Path 1, both layers, after v1:* gameplay radar extends the Sensor Spire line in the deterministic sim, and a walled “radar lab” serves as the test-bed. *Its downside:* two implementations of one physics, which need differential tests, and a map that needs a real metric scale. *Path 3, a test-bed before v1:* the radar lab is built early as a research tool. *Its downside:* it pulls effort from the game, and the fun gate and v1 slip. The owner named paths 1 and 3, so path 2 (a game feature only) is not prepared for. **What prepares for both (engineering calls):** (a) Nothing before S2’s plan depends on radar. (b) The lab would be its own walled crate (AGENTS.md §4.9). It never writes sim state and never enables the sim’s `research` feature. Its float results are not compared across operating systems, so it stays out of the cross-OS guard. A finding that graduates into play is reimplemented in the sim’s integer types. The differential test between the two uses a tolerance declared in game units. Adding the crate to `WALLED_PACKAGES` is a §5 contract change, and whether the lab ships with the game (like the client) or never ships (like `bench`) is the owner’s, so both wait for the owner’s choice of path. (c) Sensing becomes one seam. Today `sight.rs` covers spheres only, and unit vision (`programs::UNIT_VISION_RADIUS_VOXELS`) and Survey’s sightings (`survey.rs`) sit elsewhere. S2’s plan brings spheres, unit vision, pickets and Survey under one sensor interface, with two outputs: the live view the fog filter reads, and the knowledge store’s sightings and reach. S4’s Sensor Spire joins it, and radar would join it as one more sensor. (d) In-sim radar would use integer log-domain values (centibels and a lookup table) for the radar equation’s 1/R⁴ term and the wide spread of radar cross-sections, which overflow Q16.16 and Q32.32. Its Doppler would be radial velocity from per-tick position changes, not signal processing, updated at the 250 ms decision tick. The 50 ms tick itself is fixed by the spec, not a tuning value. (e) The map’s metric scale (metres per voxel) is written down before either path starts, as a rules question for the owner. It interacts with locomotion: at one metre a voxel the map is 384 m across, and units moving one to two voxels a second (item 90) would sit below a ground radar’s minimum detectable velocity. (f) A research memo, written on the owner’s request and before the owner chooses, covers: the radar equation and radar cross-section at game scale; terrain masking over voxels; Doppler and moving-target filtering; bistatic geometry; passive radar with an illuminator of opportunity; and the cost of each path. **Open for the owner with the memo:** the spec’s Pall is perpetual darkness (“Solar is a memory”) and has no day cycle. So whether a sun stands above the Pall as a radio illuminator, whether a match has a sun’s path through its day (a new rule), and how ash affects radio in the band the memo picks (long wavelengths pass; at X-band and above, ash shows as clutter and attenuates) are lore and rules questions for the owner. So is realism against fiction. Published research does use the Sun’s radio emission as a noise illuminator, but for echoes from large surfaces over long integration. Real solar passive radar would not find vehicle-sized targets within a 3-to-8-minute Push, so a physically real version would show nothing on screen. **(5) What follows.** S1’s demo review and rulings are item 139. S2’s plan carries (3)’s support rule, its three owner questions and (4) (c). S3’s plan carries (1) and its contract edits. S4’s plan carries (1) (h). The roadmap carries capture, with its `capture_beacon` entry, the physics collapse, and radar on whichever path the owner chooses.
- **Item 140, radar’s path chosen and a later roadmap addition (2026-10-14): the radar lab is built first, and its passive receiver takes further illuminators later.** Item 139 is reserved for S1’s stage-demo review and its rulings (item 138 (5)), which the main session writes; it is not written yet, so this item follows item 138 in the file, and item 141 follows this one. This is pull request #106. It changes no code, no proto and no rules row. Its contract paths are design docs under AGENTS.md §5: this log, `docs/design/README.md`, and the memo `docs/design/radar-lab-research.md`, whose appendix A holds its reference script as text (AGENTS.md §3’s two languages: no Python file is committed). The memo and this item were revised after their two reviews (contracts and architecture; numbers and sources) and the owner’s later rulings; the reviews are AI reviews, not independent review.

  **(1) Path 3.** After item 138 (4) left radar on two paths, the owner chose: “start by building radar realism to match published research. later we will try making improvements and see how the modifications work in the sim.” The main session reads these words as item 138 (4)’s path 3. The radar lab, a walled, float-allowed crate whose models reproduce published results, is built first as a test-bed; modifications are tried in it later and ported into the deterministic sim. The in-sim layer (“see how the modifications work in the sim”) is later and unscheduled: no stage holds it, and which stage gets in-sim radar is an operator question (the memo’s section 10, question 12). Item 138 (4) (a) to (e) stand. Item 138 (4) (f)’s “the cost of each path” is moot now that path 3 is chosen, and (4) below amends one sentence of item 138 (4). The memo of item 138 (4) (f), `docs/design/radar-lab-research.md`, is the lab’s plan of record. Its engineering calls (the memo’s section 10, “engineering: decide”) are decided under the owner’s standing instruction of 2026-09-14 and open to the owner’s overrule:
  - f64 throughout, with tail probabilities computed directly, under the memo’s numeric-safety rules (its section 8.7): newtypes that cannot hold bad values, non-finite numbers rejected at decode and any non-finite intermediate a typed error, one checked float-to-integer helper and no `as` on a float, every derived count capped with checked arithmetic before it is allocated, and an error enum with enumerated codes that implements `std::error::Error`. The wall lifts the cast lints for the whole crate, so the lab carries these rules itself;
  - no edge to any `pharmakos-*` crate: the lab takes a `CLIENT_WALL` line, with the list’s doc and AGENTS.md §4.9’s bullet generalised to walled crates that must not reach the core, and a lab test reads `Cargo.lock` to hold that it has no `pharmakos-*` dependency at all; it does not join `GUARDED_PACKAGES`, which forbidding the sim already makes redundant; and phase 0 adds the never-shipped check of (3) (b);
  - a later port reaches the sim through committed vectors in game units with a declared integer tolerance, kept outside `tests/golden` and named as a contract path of the port. Regenerating them is a bless-only command, and the lab’s test holds its fresh f64 values to the committed integers within a stated margin, never byte for byte, so that libm’s differences between operating systems cannot fail it. The tolerance departs from the workspace’s rule for two implementations of one spec on purpose: the sim implements a quantised approximation, not the same spec. A port’s cB rules rows are `proto/**` changes (AGENTS.md §12), and radar joins item 138 (4) (c)’s sensor interface;
  - no place in the cross-OS guard: goldens are published values with stated tolerances, and the heavy simulations are `#[ignore]`d checks run by hand, like `balance.rs`;
  - an in-crate FFT, special functions, complex least-squares solver (for ECA) and seeded generator with Gaussian sampling, before any dependency;
  - each detection function tested against its own values, never another’s. Shnidman’s 13.1217 dB is not the exact Marcum 13.1835 dB. The detectability page’s Swerling 1 value of 13.5033 dB, and its fluctuation loss of 8.1696 dB, come from Barton’s universal equation, not from Shnidman’s (whose values are 13.5805 dB and 8.2469 dB), so they wait in the memo’s “to verify” list until the lab has a Barton function;
  - the corrected `K` (225.54 dB) for MathWorks’ passive bistatic example, whose page drops its own 5 dB noise figure;
  - goldens are values read on the page (V), values reproduced from stated inputs that match a published output (V-calc), or exact or formula values that no source prints, confirmed by two independent implementations (X, a new flag). The memo’s appendix A, a stdlib-only Python script kept as text in the memo, never as a file in the tree, prints every X value. Everything else waits in the memo’s “to verify” list;
  - multipath as an optional flat-earth factor, off by default. Terrain masking over a heightmap is a stated 2.5D simplification of item 138 (4) (f)’s voxels: it loses overhangs and Mine’s tunnels, so a 3D voxel traversal comes before any masking port;
  - NREL’s SPA as the reference ephemeris and the Almanac’s low-precision formula as the second implementation;
  - a strict scenario format with units in field names and a capped, typed decoder: caps on file size, nesting depth, string and number-lexeme length and list counts, and on a heightmap’s width × height by checked multiply; duplicate keys, `/* */` comments, non-finite numbers and an out-of-range PGM `maxval` rejected; a hand-rolled seeded property test; and module-level denies on panics and unchecked arithmetic. No `serde`, no `thiserror` and no `proptest` in the lab;
  - the memo’s phase order (its section 9), with phase 0 contract-only (the decoder lands with phase 1a’s first fields), phase 1 split into 1a (the range equation), 1b (special functions) and 1c (detection), phase 4 split into 4a (the receiver site and bistatic geometry) and 4b (the cross-ambiguity function and ECA), and phase 4a depending on phase 2, since line of sight, the horizon and multipath take the site’s height.

  *Downside:* path 3’s own, as item 138 (4) recorded it: the lab pulls effort from the game, and the fun gate and v1 may slip. Item 141 (2) bounds it by running the lab beside S3.

  **(2) A later roadmap addition.** The owner added: “future future roadmap addition of secondary illuminators of opportunity - receivable by the same passive receiver that is used for catching solar ioo. different antennae configurations but same relative location, height being variable by use of tower or tethered drone”. It is roadmap, not committed scope:
  - The memo’s phase 6, after the solar phase, adds terrestrial illuminators: FM, DVB-T and the like, as entries with their EIRP, position and height, and the antenna configurations that receive them. They are received at the same site and with the same receiver as the Sun. Phase 6’s golden tests are the memo’s passive bistatic cases run through that site: MathWorks’ passive example with the noise figure restored, O’Hagan, Baker and Griffiths, Howland, Maksimiuk and Reitsma, and Pető and Seller.
  - Phase 4 does not build illuminators of opportunity. It uses those published cases only as fixtures that validate the passive chain: bare link budgets, and the cross-ambiguity function and ECA on a synthetic signal. Its illuminator set holds one generic synthetic illuminator.

  **Engineering call, binding from the start:** the passive receiver is one receiver site (the memo’s section 8.6):
  - a geodetic anchor (latitude, longitude and elevation, which SPA needs) and a local east-north-up frame in metres;
  - a height above the heightmap’s surface at the site that is a free parameter, standing for a tower or a tethered drone, from which line of sight, the radar horizon and multipath follow;
  - one or more antenna configurations, each with its own pattern, gain, band and bandwidth, sharing one phase centre, a stated simplification of the owner’s “same relative location”;
  - a set of illuminators: phase 4b’s synthetic one, then the Sun, then terrestrial transmitters.

  Phases 4a, 4b and 5 build it in that shape, so adding an illuminator is a scenario entry and not a rewrite. *Downside:* phases 4 and 5 carry some generality that phase 6, if it never runs, will not use. **Open for the owner, then ruled in (3) (d):** tethered-drone motion, the drone’s position wander and the Doppler it puts on the reference channel, is a fidelity choice; the memo recommended a static site by default, because every published passive golden is for a static receiver. The line between the two kinds of call: a choice that decides whether the lab can represent something the owner named (the tethered drone’s motion) goes to the owner; a default for a model that stays available and leaves every published golden unchanged (multipath off by default) is engineering.

- **Item 144, S2’s kickoff interview (2026-10-16): the owner’s answers, each the recommended option unless it says otherwise.** The owner said: “kick off S2”. The main session swept the spec, the record and the code for S2, then interviewed the owner on the questions that shape play, as item 127 did for S1.

  **(1) Collapse: everything on a detached region falls with it and takes one flat damage** (item 138 (3)’s first question). Units, structures and beacons alike ride the region down, and each takes the rule’s flat damage. The core’s bore is never detachable. *Downside:* one crater under a beacon can kill it, and a structure that moves changes hashed state, which is more determinism code.

  **(2) Collapse’s kill credit goes to the seat whose edit detached the region** (item 138 (3)’s second question). A crater, a charge or a dig that detaches a region credits its seat with the fall’s damage, as direct fire does; a seat’s own edit credits nobody (self-inflicted, spec section 3). *Downside:* each detach carries its seat, one more piece of hashed state.

  **(3) Mine never undermines** (item 138 (3)’s third question). Mine’s dig never detaches a region that carries any seat’s structure, extending S1’s “never dig under structures” (item 127 (9)). Sapping is the mortar’s, the charge’s and breach’s. *Downside:* no tunnel-sapping tactic in v1.

  **(4) Unit vision is a radius, with no line of sight.** A unit sees everything within its sight radius, a rules row (S1-34), as spheres do now; line of sight stays a seam in the one sensor interface (item 138 (4) (c)). *Downside:* walls and ridges hide nothing, so there is no ambush behind cover.

  **(5) Terraform: levelling sites and refilling craters.** This rules the meaning item 128 (d) and S1’s plan, decision 5, left open. Before building, a drone levels the target’s footprint to its anchor’s height: `FILL` raises it, `DIG` lowers it, and `BOTH` does both. `FILL` and `BOTH` also refill craters and trenches inside the beacon’s sphere back to the generated surface, so Build’s fill and dig undo a moat (spec section 9). Each voxel costs the wall’s cost per voxel. *Downside:* there is no free-form sculpting, and refilling competes with building for drone time.

  **(6) The nightly scenarios play Easy, and are re-baselined at S5.** Each of Rusher, Turtle and Hunter plays Easy, which carries the Balanced weighting (spec section 14), on a fixed seed set of about twenty seeds. The 65% band applies (spec section 15). S2’s close acknowledges the bands as Easy’s, and they are re-baselined when Normal lands at S5. *Downside:* an arm may beat Easy only because Easy is weak, so an early alarm can say more about Easy than about balance.

  **(7) S2 plans the whole row, with a cut order written in advance.** S2’s plan sizes the whole row honestly, with collapse, Defend and Attack and Build’s S2 settings added. It writes now what moves to S3 first if S2 runs late, so that a slip is a planned cut. *Downside:* the stage may still run long before a cut is taken.

G3′-real is therefore the named depth task (AGENTS.md §10 item 6): 300 units and 40 beacons as world totals (item 63), tick p99 at most 50% of the tick, and at least 4× speed on the headless runner (spec section 16). Its written fallback is the spec’s: a lower map power budget, and shorter segments. The owner rules the plan’s owner rows in bulk on its recommendations (item 127 (1)). Combat’s numbers are proposed inside the spec’s ranges as rules-table data and checked headless, and the owner tunes them at S2’s demo (item 127 (3)). The main session merges the plan after two adversarial reviews, under the delegation item 141 renewed, and S2’s first wave starts at once. *Downside:* lanes start before the owner has read the plan.

The owner was then interviewed on the plan’s decisions that most shape play. Decision numbers are the plan’s, sections 6 and 7.
  - **Decision 1, size:** the whole row, with section 4.5’s cuts taken only at their checkpoints (the recommended option). *Downside:* the ladder’s later stages slip by about seven plan-weeks unless absorbed, so the gate date moves.
  - **Decision 4, an unset `roe` reads as `RETURN_FIRE`,** a fifth omitted-setting default with an I-level note (the recommended option). *Downside:* it is irreversible once files omit it.
  - **Decision 5, S2-11:** in live vision a seat sees an enemy asset’s kind, position, heading and exact HP; from memory, its kind, position and the sighting’s age; never a beacon’s mandate, power, units or build progress (the recommended option). The owner added: “I want intelligence and surveillance to be a huge factor in this game.” *Downside:* exact HP is perfect information about what a seat sees, and spec section 19 lists the perfect-intel snowball as a risk.
  - **Decision 7, X-08:** “unsmoothed net worth” is held value alone, so among score-tied seats the one holding more wins, then the one that destroyed more, then the one that lost fewer beacons, then a shared win (the recommended option). *Downside:* it reverses S1’s reading, and a builder beats a raider on a tie.
  - **The cut order: Survey is never cut.** Section 4.5’s third cut, Survey’s refresh pass, leaves the cut order, so full Survey ships in S2 whatever happens, and any further cut is the owner’s (the recommended option, put to the owner after decision 5’s answer). *Downside:* there is one planned cut fewer if S2 runs late.
  - **Decision 41, targeting:** the autocannon fires at the nearest enemy unit, else the nearest enemy structure or beacon. The mortar fires at the enemy asset in range with the most enemy assets inside its splash, and never where its splash holds an own asset. Enemy wall voxels are targets only for a breach: an Attack beacon with `breach_allowed` asks the seat’s mortars in range to shell the first wall column on its route, and sends its charge (the recommended option). *Downside:* a seat with no Attack beacon never breaches a wall.
  - **Decisions 40 and 10, walls and blasts: per-material hardness, against the recommendation.** A wall target is a box of voxels at `wall_cost_per_voxel` each, at least two voxels high. A wall voxel cracks, then breaks. A demolition charge cuts flat down to the wall’s footing, so its gap is walkable; mortar craters stay balls. Bedrock and the core’s bore are never removed. Beyond the recommendation, terrain materials resist a blast by material too: stone takes more blasts than dirt, by a per-material blast-level row the plan proposes. *Downside:* more rows and a tuning surface before the duel report exists.
  - **Decision 35, Easy’s Defend guard on its commander, moves from S5 to S2:** Easy adds the guard in the round after a Push in which its commander died (the recommended option). *Downside:* an operator behaviour lands three stages before Normal and Hard share it, at about half an agent-day.
  - **Decision 9, the demolition charge’s carrier:** a raider of an Attack beacon with `breach_allowed` loads a charge at `$` 15 when the breach needs one and plants it at the breach point; a carrier killed before it plants drops a charge that never fires (the recommended option). *Downside:* the raider’s role widens, and Build cannot place a charge.
  - **Decision 43, repair’s price:** restoring hit points costs that share of the asset’s build cost, filed under the Quartermaster’s Repair band; the commander is repaired free (the recommended option). *Downside:* repair can starve building in a war, and a seat with no money has drones standing beside damaged structures.
  - **Decision 37, a collapse several seats cut:** its credit is split equally among the distinct seats whose edits that tick removed a voxel next to the region, by largest remainder, ties to the lowest seat (the recommended option). *Downside:* a seat that chipped one voxel shares equally with the seat whose charge did the work.

Decision 32 thereby grants the main session a new authority, separate from item 141’s merge delegation: it takes a planned cut of section 4.5 at that cut’s checkpoint, and any further cut is the owner’s. *Downside:* those decisions pass on the recommendation until S2’s demo shows them.

S2’s demo shows a collapse only in a staged headless run, and says so. The rule is ready when later terrain makes collapse reachable. *Downside:* about 6.5 agent-days for something players will not see in S2.

  **(3) Process rules the merges taught.**
  - **A lane takes `main` only by a signed merge, never by a rebase or a force-push:** `git fetch origin main`, `git merge --no-ff --no-commit FETCH_HEAD`, then `git commit -s`. The desktop app’s Auto-fix needs a branch whose pushed history is never rewritten, and the DCO walk checks merge commits as it checks every other. For a pushed branch this replaces the rebase that four harness texts still describe, and the coming harness pull request (S2’s plan, section 4.6) rewords all four:
    - AGENTS.md §6, “Rebase on `main` before opening a PR”;
    - `scripts/merge-train.sh`, which rebase-merges each PR and rebases the next lane’s worktree with `--force-with-lease` (~19–21), and refuses a branch with merge commits (~53, ~188);
    - CLAUDE.md’s local-verify path (~76), “green on its rebase onto `main`”;
    - `.claude/workflows/wave-lanes.js` (~106), “when the main session’s merge train rebases it”.

    Until that pull request merges, `scripts/merge-train.sh` is out of use as a whole: its default mode rebase-merges each PR and rebases and force-pushes the next lane, and `--local-verify` refuses a branch with merge commits, which every lane branch now carries. The main session merges each PR by a merge commit, once CI’s checks are green on its head after its merge of `main`. *Downside:* a lane’s history carries merge commits that a reader of the PR reads past, and the merge train’s automation is out of use until the harness pull request.
    - **The force-pushes, recorded.** `base`’s merge of `con3`, `6b27e68`, had no sign-off. It was reworded to `34e6db7` with its tree unchanged (`9858e95`), and the branch was force-pushed once to replace it. `night` also reordered its own commits once with `--force-with-lease`, before any merge of `main`, as its fix pass.
  - **No lane kills a process it did not start,** restating item 113’s rule, which `wave-lanes.js`’ lane brief already carries. A lane that finds a build, a test run or a Godot process in its way waits for it or says so; it never stops another lane’s or the owner’s. *Downside:* a lane can sit behind a hung process until the main session clears it.
  - **`--no-verify` is for genuine emergencies only** (AGENTS.md §8). It was used twice: once in a local rebuild in `base`, and once on a rebase in `vfy1`, where no hook existed to skip. Nothing unchecked was pushed, and the rule is restated in every lane brief. *Downside:* none beyond the rule’s own.

  **(2) The owner’s rulings of 2026-10-20, and the owner’s answers to this entry’s rules review.**
  - **Seat-sight targeting.** Every weapon, the core’s autocannon included, chooses only a target its own seat sees that tick under the sim’s sensor seam (`World::seen_by`, E10); range stays the weapon’s squared-distance test; `RETURN_FIRE` answers only an attacker the seat sees; the mortar’s friendly-fire check stays on ground truth; a shell in flight lands regardless. Built in #129. It amends decisions 8, 21 and 41, whose “nearest” and “in range” now mean among the enemy assets the seat sees that tick, and E12. *Downside:* a weapon whose range passes its seat’s sight, the mortar’s 40 against its own vision of 12 and a sphere’s 24, fires to its full range only where another sensor sees.
  - **`RETURN_FIRE` is literal everywhere:** fire only at an asset that damaged one of the seat’s own within the window; a raider on it never starts a fight or raids. **An unset `roe` reads `FREE_FIRE` on a Defend and on an Attack beacon, and `RETURN_FIRE` on Build, Mine and Survey** (the owner’s answer to finding 23, widening the ruling’s first form, which named Attack alone). `dfnd` adds the Defend arm to `Roe::of_setting`, `atk` the Attack arm, `vfy3` makes the I0003 note and its Fix read the default by writ, and the next `proto/**` pull request brings `playbook.proto`’s header comment to it. This amends decision 4 (item 144 (11)), which read an unset `roe` as `RETURN_FIRE` on every writ; it is reversible, since no shipped file can hold a Defend beacon’s settings before `dfnd` or an Attack beacon’s before `atk`. *Downside:* the default differs by writ, which the note has to say.
  - **Footings.** From the tick a structure’s construction begins, or a beacon is placed, every voxel of its footprint columns, bedrock to the top of the map, ignores every edit (shells, charges, digs, terraform) and counts as anchored ground for the support rule; a building falls only by losing HP, and nothing undermines it or lands on it. Ruins and seat walls are not covered. A *footing* is a live structure’s or beacon’s footprint column; “the wall’s footing” of decision 40 is a wall’s base, which footings do not cover. The rule generalises the core’s bore exclusion (E31), is being built by `site` (#133, open), and supersedes `fall`’s question whether a dig may drop a region onto a building. **This amends item 144 (1): structures and beacons stand on footings and no longer ride a region down; units, wrecks and ruins still do.** *Downside:* no building is ever undermined, so a collapse carries only units, the commander, wrecks and ruins.
  - **Repair and walls (`site`).**
    - **The per-beacon funds** for repair and for voxel work are an owner-ruled amendment of spec §7’s Treasury row, “no per-beacon pools”. Work is paid in advance because the Quartermaster fills one request per beacon per decision tick, while repair and voxel work happen tick by tick; a beacon’s top-up is `TOP_UP_TICKS` of its drones’ work, a PLACEHOLDER (`docs/placeholders.md`’s S2-19). The funds count in held value, return to the treasury whole on a mandate switch or a recycle (#133’s `World::return_site_funds`, as its head builds it), and **are lost when the beacon is destroyed** (the owner’s answer to finding 25), as a structure going up is lost.
    - **Walls follow the two settings every structure does:** a cracked own wall voxel is repaired below `repair_threshold_pct`; a removed one is rebuilt only under `rebuild_destroyed`, with no separate refill. This amends decision 42.
    - **Repairability is consistent:** every own structure is repairable, beacons and walls included, with units and the commander.
    - **A half-built structure paused by a mandate switch resumes only when the beacon is Build again and a Build row names its target again** (the owner’s answer to finding 24), since a switch clears the old targets (spec §5). A switch is not decision 26’s drop: decision 26 rules a paid target removed from a Build list, while a switch leaves no list to remove it from.
    - #133’s head still builds the readings in its owner questions 2 to 4 (refill while the target stands, no beacon repair, a switch strands); `site` changes them to this ruling before it merges.
  - **CI budget.** The Windows `cargo xtask ci` leg reached 77 min on `main` at #129’s merge (run 39471415164) and 83 min at #131’s (run 39506130625), over item 119 (5)’s 75. Item 116 (6) (f)’s question, a `[profile.*]` change or a split, fell due with it, and the owner chose the split: the test step sharded into two or three parallel jobs per OS, the budget kept (a `.github` and `xtask` pull request, queued: section 4.6’s CI shard row). **Item 119 (5)’s 75-minute rule is waived until the CI shard pull request merges** (the owner’s answer to finding 22), and no new heavy test or scenario lands meanwhile. *Downside:* `main`’s Windows leg stays over its budget for a few merges.
  - **Roadmap, not S2:** ammunition, as a hauled resource produced and carried by drones, with the deferred logistics delivery (S4 or later; S2 has unlimited ammunition); and some materials, dirt first, *displaceable but not destroyable*: a blast or dig moves those voxels rather than deleting them (stage unset; open: where the dirt goes, which materials, terraform’s use of it, and rims in pathing).
  - **A term:** the owner coined **FAIBAI**, “For AI, By AI”, after FUBU, for work written by AI for AI to read and act on (AGENTS.md, the lane briefs, the reviews, and v1.1’s agent-facing gateway and `llms.txt`).

- **Item 158, the owner's ruling on P1's QUICK bar, and where lanes build (2026-11-12).** (1) is the owner's ruling. (2) to (4) are engineering calls by the main session under the standing "go with your recommendations", each open to the owner's overrule. The AI review is not independent review.
  - **(1) QUICK is made fast at its source: no fallback, and no change to the size unit.**
    - **What `vfyq`'s first run found.** `vfyq` (item 157 (9)) stopped without a pull request, on its own stop condition. QUICK's cost is linear in a playbook's bytes, and nothing in it is quadratic. About 70% of it is outside the verifier: `crates/proto`'s JSON codec (`json::read`, then JSON to wire to prost) and the plan fingerprint (prost encode, wire to JSON, write, xxh3). The verifier's own walks are about 22%, mostly building a JSON Pointer string at every node. A size unit bounds neither the condition nodes (up to `CONDITION_MAX_NODES`, 24, per condition) nor the bytes.
    - **The figures**, on the owner's machine, with a release build, an uncommitted harness in `crates/bench` and 200 timed calls (p50/p99):
      - `budget_128`: QUICK 1.62/2.24 ms.
      - Item 157 (7)'s shape (63 handlers with 24-node conditions; 127 units, 79 KB): QUICK 14.5/28.4 ms, FULL 20.2/35.9 ms.
      - 127 route steps, each with a 24-node `skip_if` (127 units, 151 KB): QUICK 21.8/35.6 ms, FULL 20.2/35.0 ms. This is the larger case.
      - Lazy pointers alone, in the codec and the verifier, were projected at about 11–12 ms p99.
    - **The ruling.** The owner was asked how S3 closes the gate. The options were P1's written fallback, a cap on condition nodes, charging conditions in size units, or recording the miss. The owner's answers were "proceed - use C:", then "i did mean c: - not option c", and "i want this to be built well and built efficiently - which was our original plan".
    - **What follows.** The fallback is not taken, and item 94's unit stands: conditions still count nothing. The original plan of item 157 (9) stands, a lane that makes QUICK meet 5 ms. Its scope widens to where the time actually goes.
    - **Recorded honestly.** The main session first read "C:" as the third option, and drafted a lane that charged conditions. That draft was discarded before it was pushed.
  - **(2) `vfyq`, reopened with a wider grant.**
    - **What it owns.** `crates/verifier`, and `crates/proto`'s JSON codec (`src/json/`), which nobody else edits while it runs. It also holds a named place, the plan fingerprint's computation in `crates/sim/src/hash.rs`. That file is determinism code (AGENTS.md §5), so the PR names it.
    - **What it does.** It builds JSON Pointers only where a diagnostic needs one. It allocates less. It drops the intermediate wire layer wherever text can go straight to prost with the same results. It computes the fingerprint from bytes QUICK already holds instead of re-encoding the playbook three times. Any other gain it measures goes in too.
    - **What it holds byte-identical.** Every output: every fingerprint (a save stamps them), every `report_hash`, every golden, and the canonical form. So no `VERIFIER_VERSION` change and no chain moves.
    - **How that is proved.** A differential property test feeds the old and the new fingerprint, and the old and the new decode, the same generated playbooks, and asserts equal bytes or the same typed error. It is kept until the old path is deleted, and committed vectors replace it then. A counted-work or allocation bound pins QUICK on both shapes.
    - **The target.** QUICK at or under 5 ms p99 on both shapes in (1) and on `budget_128`, with FULL no slower. It is measured on an idle machine with at least 2,000 timed calls per shape, because the owner's machine is noisy at p99.
    - **If 5 ms is still out of reach** after this work, the lane reports the figures and where the remaining time goes, and the main session takes it to the owner with options.
  - **(3) Where it runs.** `vfyq` runs after `lic` merges (it shares `crates/sim`) and before `bench3`. `bench3`'s P1 harness carries both shapes in (1). Estimated at 4 agent-days, up from 1.5.
  - **(4) Lane builds move to the C: drive.** The owner said "use C:".

    - D:'s other folders are left as they are.
    - Item 157 (9)'s hold on the cut checkpoints stands until the owner says how lanes run with C: in use.
  - **(5) `VERIFIER_VERSION` re-sequenced on `lic`'s review.** `lic` moves a verdict (a Spire queue is no longer E0009), and the plan bumps the version whenever verdicts move, so `lic` takes 0.1.0-s3.2, `vfy6` 0.1.0-s3.3 and `pred` 0.1.0-s3.4. `vfyq` moves no verdict and takes none.

  - **(1) The rule as recorded (the main session's call).** A tracked file outside `library/` that reproduces a library template's expression carries the library's licence beside its own as ONE combined expression, `GPL-3.0-or-later AND (MIT OR Apache-2.0)`; where a file in a permissively licensed area carries no game expression, the library's `MIT OR Apache-2.0` alone. Expression is a sentence of at least 8 words ending in a full stop, or a run of at least 12 consecutive words of one library string (`MIN_WORDS` and `RUN_WORDS` in `xtask/src/licence_quotes.rs`); a title, a name or a step label is below both. **The line is one the main session drew, not a finding about copyright:** below it a file is treated as quoting no expression, a contributor may always add the library's licence to a file below it (the check demands it only above it), and the owner can move the line. The reason is the project's own rule: the game's licence had been applied alone to text the project offers under `library/`'s terms, and PR #189's review found three render goldens missing from `REUSE.toml`'s by-name list. No legal conclusion is drawn from it.

  - **(2) The profile.** The root `Cargo.toml` puts `pharmakos-sim` and every third-party package (`[profile.dev.package."*"]`) at `opt-level = 2`, with debug assertions and overflow checks on. `pharmakos-proto` is not named and stays at 0 (optimising it saves about 0.4 ms per world load), and each package of the godot family (reachable from the walled client's `godot` dependency and from no other member except through it: gdextension-api, glam, godot, godot-bindings, godot-cell, godot-codegen, godot-core, godot-ffi, godot-macros, heck, nanoserde, nanoserde-derive, venial) has a named table at 0. The allocation test is the one claim the optimiser weakens, so it runs as an invocation of its own with the sim at 0 (`--config 'profile.dev.package.pharmakos-sim.opt-level=0'`), exempt for exactly the (package, target) pairs of `UNOPTIMISED_OWNERS`.
  - **(3) Every build xtask makes to test, hash or ship is read back from cargo's own report** (`xtask/src/resolved.rs`), through one door, `resolved::execute`, and fails if a workspace unit has debug assertions or overflow checks off, the sim or a crate it runs is at 0, a godot-family crate is optimised, or any other third-party crate is at 0. The `determinism` build is held to `[profile.release]`'s optimisation, set nowhere else (an `opt-level` in `release-checked`'s own tables is refused), with the sim's library built. `cargo xtask package` takes the library and `gamectl` from the build's report, and a stale file at a conventional path cannot be zipped. What codegen can change behind the report is pinned or refused: every checked call sets `CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS` and `CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTDOCFLAGS`, names `rustc` and `rustdoc` by their plain names, turns both rustc wrappers off (`--config`, and empty `RUSTC_WRAPPER` and `RUSTC_WORKSPACE_WRAPPER`), and removes `RUSTC_BOOTSTRAP`; a non-empty flags, compiler, wrapper, `RUSTC_BOOTSTRAP`, `CARGO_TARGET_<triple>_` runner or linker variable is refused by name before anything builds. A compiler cache wrapper is not used on this project's machines or in CI.
  - **(4) Tests run through xtask's own runner** (`xtask/src/runner.rs`, the hidden `__run-test`). Every checked test call carries one `--config target.<host>.runner='<xtask> __run-test'` string, named relative to cargo's working folder when xtask lies under it, absolute otherwise. A string, not an array: measured with cargo 1.98.1, an array is merged with a config file's array in an order that varied, and a string replaces a file's string for the triple and for a `cfg(...)`. The runner writes one record per start (a file of its own, `create_new`, in a folder fresh for the run under the target directory) and then runs the test with its status passed through. The judgment is the set of executables the build reported against the set the runner started, compared as paths without touching the disk: a step fails when a reported test target did not run, or ran from a file the build did not report. Nothing reads what cargo or libtest print, so a test's output passes through as bytes. The target directory is the trust boundary: xtask defends against a stale file at a conventional path and claims nothing more, since whoever can write the target directory can replace xtask. Doctests go through the same runner, with one process per doctest: rustdoc leaves `RUSTDOC_DOCTEST_BIN_PATH` unset under any runner, so the merged bundle ran every doctest in one process, and a doctest calling `exit(0)` hid a failing one. The checked doctest call marks the run (`PHARMAKOS_XTASK_DOCTEST_RUN=1`) and the runner then sets that variable per start; `xtask/tests/doctest_runner.rs` holds rustdoc to it with a real failing doctest beside an exiting one. A doctest run is held to cargo's exit status, since how many doctests start cannot be known from the build.
  - **(5) The linker is pinned per host triple, and rustc wrappers are off, in xtask and in the repository's cargo config.** Every checked call and every clippy call carries `--config target.<host>.linker="<default>"` from one table, `DEFAULT_LINKERS` (`link.exe` on x86_64-pc-windows-msvc; `cc` on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, which is WSL's host too, and on aarch64-apple-darwin). `.cargo/config.toml` holds the same table and the same two empty wrapper keys, and tests hold the file equal to xtask's table, reading it (and `rust-toolchain.toml`) with a strict reader (`strict_toml`) that refuses any line or value shape it does not know, so a linker or wrapper cannot be spelled where the tests do not look. The reason is cargo's fingerprint: the linker and an empty wrapper are hashed into a unit's metadata, so two settings would make `cargo xtask` and a plain `cargo` rebuild each other's units (measured, with no rebuild across alternating runs on Windows and Linux). Consequence: inside this repository a user-level linker or wrapper setting does not apply. `cargo xtask` builds, lints and runs tests on the three CI host triples; on another host a plain `cargo` works, and `cargo xtask` refuses when it builds, lints or runs tests (the checked calls, clippy, the runner's configuration and `package` ask for the host; a bare `fmt`, `deny`, `reuse` or `buf` does not), naming the row to add to `DEFAULT_LINKERS`. A contributor on another host runs plain `cargo`, or adds the host's row to xtask's table and to `.cargo/config.toml` once rustc's default linker there is checked. No unverified row is added. This is a support policy a contributor meets: decided; the owner can veto.
  - **(6) The running xtask is never a file a build writes.** The `xtask` and `ci` aliases in `.cargo/config.toml` build xtask with `--profile xtask`, a profile of its own (`[profile.xtask] inherits = "dev"` in the root `Cargo.toml`), so the running binary lies in `<target>/xtask/`. The `test` step builds xtask's binary into `<target>/debug/` for `doctest_runner`; before the profile, a build with other settings replaced the running file (Windows: access denied; Linux: the next invocation found it deleted). A runner whose executable is gone is refused with that cause.
  - **(7) The toolchain is checked at the door, for every command but the hidden runner.** Before any command runs (`__run-test`, which cargo starts, is dispatched first), the compiler the pinned `rustc` resolves to and the `cargo` xtask runs (`$CARGO`) must each report `rust-toolchain.toml`'s channel as their `release:` (`check_toolchain`), so `cargo +other xtask` is refused before any step, naming both releases. What it does not prove (the module doc says so): a custom toolchain reporting the same release passes, because the toolchain's own files are on the trusted side of the boundary.
  - **(8) A path cargo cannot be given as a runner is refused when a plan that runs `test` or `test-research` starts**, before fmt, clippy or deny (`runner_config_for`, `runner_spelling`); cargo splits a runner on whitespace. The refusal is on xtask's own path (`<target>/xtask/xtask`): it holds whitespace or a quote in both its checkout-relative spelling (used when it lies under the checkout) and its absolute one, which is the case for a target folder outside the checkout whose path holds one. A checkout under a folder with a space, with the target inside it, is accepted. Neither `fmt` nor `clippy` alone needs the runner, so neither refuses.
  - **(9) The `profiles` step** holds `overflow-checks` on for every profile in both files by the scan of the root `Cargo.toml` and `.cargo/config.toml`, and fails on a `[profile.*]` line it cannot read.   - **(2) One door for every snapshot (decided; the owner can veto).** `Snapshot::door` (crate-internal) returns `Closed<'w>`, a token that borrows the world, and only a world between ticks with its graph settled passes; it refuses with `Unclosed::MidTick` or `Unclosed::Unsettled`. `Snapshot::through` copies the world the token holds, so the borrow checker refuses a change between the door and the copy. `Snapshot::capture` and `Runner::capture` return `Result<Snapshot, SnapshotError>` (`SnapshotError::MidTick`, and the new `SnapshotError::Unsettled`), and `Runner::new` returns `Result<Runner, SnapshotError>`. `Snapshot::through` (copy the world a token holds) and `Snapshot::restore_closed` (restore, and hand back the token for the restored world) are new; `restore_into` keeps its signature and is `restore_closed` with the token dropped. A segment's freeze answers a refusal as `TickError::MidTick` or the new `TickError::Unsettled`. `Host::open` answers a refusal as the gateway's existing internal error, with no new gateway variant. Read from the diff against `70560e36`: neither the snapshot's format nor the state hash changed (no column or field added; the diff of `snapshot.rs` adds the door, its tokens and `SnapshotError::Unsettled`, and changes `capture`'s signature; `restore_into` keeps its own), because the pending set is empty at every closed tick and so there is nothing to save. No save of an earlier build is migrated: the PR body says none has been published.
  - **(3) A lobby layout passes the door once, before placement, and placement cannot unsettle it by type (decided; the owner can veto).** `Snapshot::door_for_layout` (`snapshot.rs`) hands back `ClosedForLayout`, which holds the world mutably for one thing, the placement (`crate::layout::place`, moved out of `World` in what it does). Placement reaches the world only through `crate::layout::Placement` (`layout/placement.rs`), whose world is a private field of that child module, exposing the reads and the constructors placement uses (`place_beacon`, `set_attack`, `fabricate`) and nothing else, none of which writes the open phase or the repairer, the two things the door reads. A graph waiting for its repair is refused as the new `LayoutRefused::Unsettled` and nothing is placed; no door refusal can follow placement, because there is no second door (placement's own refusals, such as `NoRoom`, remain). `Host::seed_layout_with_settings` answers it as its existing internal error; the host method is a harness seam no wire method reaches, so the variant reaches no JSON-RPC answer, audit line, save or golden.
  - **(4) The breach search (decided; the owner can veto).** It keeps the pathfinder's second cost mode of E23 and changes what it reads. **What item 62 said:** search nodes are ordered `(f, h, node_id)`, ascending in all three, so the pop sequence is a function of the graph and nothing else. **What is extended:** the breach search's order is `(f, h, state)` with the layer inside the state id (`node * 2 + crossed`) and a fixed neighbour order, still total; the heuristic of an uncrossed state adds the crossing's `BREACH_COLUMN_COST`, which every way from it still pays, so it stays admissible and consistent and every answer is the same (the PR body's states expanded per search: `breach-and-raze` 6,918 to 3,108, `mortar-breaks-wall` 533 to 48, `breach-at-a-corner` 7,305 to 3,288). The search is over (column, crossed):
    - Uncrossed, its moves are the walkers' own, `Surface::neighbour`'s, along and down enemy wall tops included.
    - The crossing is one step by the surface's own rule, `Surface::step_over` (the endpoints at a height the caller gives, a diagonal's two sides read where a walker stands), from a column a walker stands on that is no breachable wall onto a breachable wall column read at its footing. It names the wall, and the plant is the column stepped from, which a walker from the start reaches by construction. It costs `BREACH_COLUMN_COST` on top of the step.
    - Crossed, its moves are the step rule over footings and tops, each breachable column entered costing `BREACH_COLUMN_COST` more.
    - The start has no special case. The goal is taken only crossed.
    - The search is handed a `SealedWay`, which only `SealedWay::of` makes (the sealing oracle's verdict), so it has no "open" answer. `BreachRefused::NoWall` and its counter are removed; what is left is `Exhausted` (the search spent `BREACH_EXPANSIONS` closed states before it could tell) and `NoWay` (it finished and no way that crosses a wall reaches the goal). Every refusal ends the attack `Ended::Sealed`, counted under its reason; the old "the force walks on" arm is gone.

  - **(3) `E0114`, and the principle it serves (decided; the owner can veto).** A playbook that qualifies compiles, for every rules table the verifier accepts; this is pinned by a seeded property over generated tables and generated edits (`every_two_node_edit_that_qualifies_compiles_under_every_rules_table`, with the one-node and the `PlanError` probes beside it), not proved. `E0114` (ERROR, family limits and required blocks, raised at the structure stage, so at QUICK) refuses a route of more steps than the sim's `MAX_ROUTE_STEPS` (256, read from the sim and written nowhere else, as `E0113` reads `MAX_HANDLERS`), pointing at the first step past it. The second half is the rules table's door: `Input::new` calls `Rates::check_rows(size_budget_units)` and refuses a table with `RulesGap::RowPastTheSim`, because the worst interface row a playbook within the budget can write, `switch_mandate + edit_settings_max + build_target x size_budget_units` (a Build target is one size unit, every other row is one rate, an `i32` already), must be at most `i32::MAX` ms, which is what the sim's `Row::duration_ms` sums and its compile refuses past (`PlanError::RowTooLong`). The refusal names the row as the sim sums it, its three rates, the budget and the sum. Every sum in `interface`, `estimate`, `walking` and the prose is wide (`WideMs(i128)`, the walking leg in `u128`) and cannot overflow by the types' stated bounds, and the saturating sites in those sums are gone (the sites left, each with its proof, are listed in the pull request's body). The verifier's `read_rules` is every rules check it makes in one call, and the host calls it once, at its start and before anything is written: `Host::open` and `serve::run_in` (right after the config line, before `MatchCache::open` or `reopen`) refuse a table the verifier refuses with `INVALID_ARGUMENT`, "this rules table hosts no match, because the verifier refuses it", so a refused start leaves the data root empty and announces nothing; `gamectl host`, `scenario run` and `seat doctor` all meet it, and `host`'s exit-code table gains "a rules table the verifier refuses" under exit 2. **What is not done:** the sim's own rules loader (`crates/sim/src/rules.rs`) carries no bound on the interface rates at this head, the sim is not this lane's, and a table the verifier refuses still loads in the sim; bounding the rates there is carried to the next sim lane.
  - **(4) The patch dialect (decided; the owner can veto).** `patch_plan`'s patches (and a fix's `json_patch`) are a dialect stricter than RFC 6902, on purpose: a member the editor did not mean is a mistake to report, not to drop. **This narrows a sentence of the spec, and it is told straight.** Spec v0.6 says "Edits are JSON Patches with inverse-patch undo" (`docs/spec/pharmakos-spec-v0.6.html`, about line 635) and that diagnostics carry "JSON Patch suggestions" (about line 559). As built: the forward patch is RFC 6902's six operations read more strictly, and it REFUSES an unknown member where RFC 6902 section 4 says such members are ignored; the undo is not an RFC 6902 patch at all, since each of its operations is an `add`, `remove` or `replace` plus an `undo` member, which only this gateway applies. This narrows the spec's sentence on the main session's ruling, without the owner's word on it (decided; the owner can veto; the main session tells the owner on 2026-11-21). The gateway is internal in v1 and v1.1 publishes it (AGENTS.md section 2), so the form becomes a public wire format then, which is why it is recorded here by name. The forward operations are RFC 6902's six, a `move` onto itself changes nothing, and what the dialect refuses is typed, as `Malformed` (a reading refusal) or `Bound` (a bound on the work one call does): `Malformed::PointerEscape` ("a JSON Pointer's `~` is followed by `0` or `1` (RFC 6901), and the one at byte N is not"), `UnknownMember` ("`x` is not a member of this operation; it has ..."; an undo that takes out has no members), `MixedUndo` ("a patch is forward operations or the undo of one patch, never both"), `UndoText` (an undo's written member, item or value is not exactly one of them), `UndoSlot`, `UndoTarget`, `PointerIndex` ("an array index is `0` or digits with no leading zero and no sign (RFC 6901)", so `+1`, `01`, `-1`, an empty token and ` 1` are refused) and `EndOfArray` ("`-` names the end of an array, which only an `add`, or a `move` or `copy`'s destination, may name"); `Bound::Operations` ("this patch carries N operations, and a patch carries at most 64"), `UndoOperations` (an undo carries at most 128), `PatchText` (a patch text longer than the work bound, refused unread), `PointerTokens`, `Size`, `Depth` and `Inverse` ("this patch is not applied: the patch that would undo it could not be issued (...)"). The undo is a form of its own (`patch::Undo`, which holds an `UndoStep`: `Put`, `Take` or `Swap`): on the wire each of its operations is an `add`, `remove` or `replace` (the one that puts back, takes out or swaps) plus one member, `undo`, which carries exactly what was written (`{"op":"add","path":P,"undo":{"at":N,"jsonc":T}}`, `{"op":"remove","path":P,"undo":{}}`, `{"op":"replace","path":P,"undo":{"jsonc":T}}`), read back by the JSONC reader, which must find exactly one value, so an undo cannot write structure. It is exact through the text: applied to the patched text it gives back the original bytes, the member's slot, its comments and its key's spelling included, with both spellings of a field kept, and it is applied as it was written (never translated by spelling and never refused as writing a field twice, so a player can edit a file that writes both names and undo exactly; decode refuses such a file with `E0001` before anything seals it). The first member put into an empty container carries the container's inside trivia in front of it, so no patch drops a comment; the property `every_undo_through_its_text_gives_the_same_bytes` applies every undo to `Document::parse(patched.to_text())`. A patch whose undo could not be issued is refused up front: `apply` applies the inverse once under every bound, hands it back only if it gives the document back exactly (`restores`), and otherwise refuses the forward patch with `Bound::Inverse`; and `patch_plan` measures the request that would send the inverse back, written as a client writes it (`rpc::request_text`), and refuses the forward patch unless it travels (`frame::travels`, the frame's own limits in one place), so an undo whose request would close the seat's connection is never handed out. The bounds, each a named constant: operations `MAX_PATCH_OPERATIONS` = 64; undo operations `MAX_UNDO_OPERATIONS` = 128 (a `move` yields two undos); pointer tokens `MAX_POINTER_TOKENS` = `MAX_DEPTH` + 1 = 65 (the grammar's `MAX_DEPTH` is 64 containers); `instantiate_template`'s parameters, at most `MAX_PATCH_OPERATIONS` = 64, checked before anything is read; and the patch-text work bound `MAX_PATCH_TEXT_CHARS` = `MAX_PLAYBOOK_CHARS` x 12 x 2 + 64 x 64 = 12,587,008 characters (`MAX_PLAYBOOK_CHARS` = 524,288; 12 is the worst escape, a surrogate pair written as two `\uXXXX` escapes), sized so that one operation whose value and path each fit the playbook's cap is never refused for its escapes, and named a bound on the work and not on legality. A patched document is held to the playbook's cap and to the grammar's depth, and the inverse to at most the cap in paths and text. Array indices are RFC 6901's (`0|[1-9][0-9]*`), read by one typed reader, `jsonc::rfc6901_index`, on every path of every operation. **The frame now bounds an edit.** Because `patch_plan` refuses a forward patch whose undo request would not fit (`frame::travels`), the frame limit decides which large edits are accepted: the PR body's case is a 205,827-byte file and `remove /routes`, whose undo request is about 336 KB. The frame size is a hardening PLACEHOLDER that item 162 (1) leaves open (`crates/gateway/src/frame.rs`: "PLACEHOLDER: the largest message, 256 KiB — owner, at hardening, alongside the rate limits" and "PLACEHOLDER: the largest frame, as [`MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES`] — owner, at hardening"), so a different size at hardening changes which large edits are accepted. Neither number is changed here, and `cert3` records what a player sees past the limit (item 162 (1)). **The caps refuse nothing the game ships:** no template in `library/` has more than 64 parameters (the most is 4, in `raid_an_enemy_beacon.jsonc`), and the client composes its own patches one operation at a time (`crates/client-gdext/src/editor.rs`, `rule_list.rs` and `vocabulary.rs`), so the 64-operation and 64-parameter bounds are not met by a shipped template or a client edit; a verifier Fix's patch is the verifier's own, and its operation count was not measured.
  - **(5) Player text reaches a person only quoted (decided; the owner can veto).** Every sentence that can carry a player's text in proto, plan-core, the verifier and the gateway is built through one door, by type; `gamectl` escapes its leaves (held by `crates/gamectl/tests/shown.rs`); and the client's and the operator's lax readers strip comments themselves (`strip_comments` in `crates/client-gdext/src/editor.rs` and `crates/operator/src/wire.rs`), to learn a shape or draw it, with the verdict the verifier's. `Quoted` is what `quoted()` returns: the text escaped, capped at `MAX_QUOTED_CHARS` (64) characters, the rest shown as an ellipsis. `Said` is text a person is shown, built from a `&'static str`, a number, a `char`, a `Quoted`, another `Said` or an engine error's words, and never from a `String`; `said!` composes them, checking its template's `{}` count at compile time. The hidden-character table, `json::grammar::HIDDEN`, is data: 44 ascending, disjoint, merged ranges covering 4,339 code points, each row naming what puts it in, the union of two sources, each named in its doc with its version: General Category Cc, Cf, Zl and Zp and the noncharacters, in Unicode 16.0.0 (`HIDDEN_UNICODE_VERSION`, from Python 3.14.4's `unicodedata` under WSL2), and `Default_Ignorable_Code_Point` in Unicode 15.0.0 (`HIDDEN_DEFAULT_IGNORABLE_VERSION`, from Perl 5.40.1's `unicore/lib/DI/Y.pl` under WSL2, read offline). That reaches the controls, the direction marks, embeddings, overrides and isolates, the zero-width characters, the tag characters, the variation selectors and the Hangul fillers; the doc says no data on the machine carries the property for 16.0, so a change 16.0 made, if any, is not in it. Only the ranges, which are facts, are committed. A character of the table is shown as `\uXXXX`. **Quoting never rewrites the file's bytes** (`quoting_never_rewrites_the_files_bytes`): it governs what a person is shown, and the player's text, sealed or saved, is as written. What the type system holds and what the scans hold, as the pull request's body states them and as `crates/plan-core/tests/door.rs`'s module doc does, and no more: the type system holds that a `Said` is built only from a `&'static str`, a number, a `char`, a `Quoted`, an `EngineWords` type's words or another `Said`, with no `From<String>` and a private field; that `Quoted`'s field is private; that the three refusal types (`json::Error`, plan-core's `Error` and the gateway's `Error`) have no public field, read through getters; and that `Said::compose` is private. The scans hold: no identifier `leak`, `into_raw` or `forget` behind the door, with string contents and comments dropped; every `static` behind the door is on a reviewed list of six; `EngineWords` and its seal (`door::EngineSeal`) are named, as identifiers, only in a crate behind the door's `src`, so an implementation, an alias or any other use outside is refused (a seal other crates must name cannot be closed by the type system across crates, since any crate that can name it could implement it); and `said!`'s `compose_checked` (public and `#[doc(hidden)]`, because a macro must call a public function) is called by the macro alone. The doors left, each with why it cannot carry player text, are `Said::engine_error` (capped at `MAX_ENGINE_CHARS`), which takes only a type that declares `EngineWords` with its reason, and `From<&'static str>`, literals only (the type holds `&'static str`, and the leak scan keeps a leaked `String` out); `Said::made_here(String)` is `pub(crate)` in proto, so the "built only from" claim holds outside the proto crate; `PlanError` and the verifier's `ProjectionError` carry playbook ids and do not declare, and are said from their fields. In the gateway the sim's `PlanError` is said in one module, `surface/plan_words.rs` (`plan_refusal`: one sentence per variant, no wildcard, every player-text field quoted, the sim's words otherwise): the type's name and every sim function that refuses with one (`compile`, `beacon_spec_of`, `duration_ms`, `InterfaceTimes`) are named only there and on the one compile site in `planning.rs`, no `format!`, `format_args!`, `write!`, `to_string`, `Debug` or `Display` is written in that file, and `tests/confinement.rs` holds all of it (the sim is not touched). `gamectl`'s printed lines escape only the leaves (an operand the user typed, a path, a scenario's or event's name, a pointer) and never a sentence gamectl composed, so its multi-line reports keep their lines and columns; `gamectl verify` prints a pointer token by token (`quoted_pointer`), so a pointer of the schema's names comes back whole however long, and only a token that is the player's own text is escaped and capped.
  - **(6) The stack (decided; the owner can veto).** Every recursion over a playbook is bounded by the grammar's depth, and a bound on depth is a bound on the stack only once the stack is a stated number, so every thread of `gamectl` and the gateway that reads player text is made by `pharmakos_plan_core::stack::player_text_thread` on `PLAYER_TEXT_STACK` = 4 MiB: `gamectl`'s `main` for every command (one `gamectl` thread), the gateway's surface thread (every method, every in-process seat), its connection threads (every frame), its dispatcher, and its accept threads (which read no text). No other thread is made in either crate (both confinement tests check it), the surface, dispatcher and accept threads are made before the announce line, a thread that cannot be made is a typed `Internal` error, and a connection thread the system will not make hangs up on its peer, is counted always, under `DropReason::NoConnectionThread`, and audited as a 503 refusal when the queue has room. What was measured when the number was set (2026-11-20, Windows, MSVC, a debug build, bisected to 4 KiB): the deepest accepted playbook needs at most 322 KiB through every planning method's door in the gateway (mostly the hosted match, the same at any depth), 259 KiB through `gamectl verify` and 259 KiB through every reader, writer and renderer in plan-core, about 3.6 KiB a container, after the grammar's leaf work and the codec's scalar arms were moved out of the recursion (parse 5.8 to 2.3 KiB a container, decode 10.6 to 3.6); the tests (`stack.rs` in plan-core, the gateway and `gamectl`) run the deepest accepted text, and one level past it, on half the constant in a debug build, which is more than six times the worst figure.
  - **(7) Counters and logs.** A connection the host drops before serving it is counted under an enumerated reason, `serve::DropReason` (`OverCapacity`, `NoConnectionThread`), whether or not the audit queue has room for the refusal's own line, and the host's audit log closes with one line per reason, zero included: `connections dropped over_capacity: <n>` and `connections dropped no_connection_thread: <n>`. The counts are the host's own (the process-wide counter and `serve::dropped` are gone), read from the closed log, and the audit log is what the gateway already shows an operator, so there is no proto or wire change; if `gamectl host` is killed, the counts of its last run are lost with it, which is accepted. The work meter (`json::work`) that pins the readers' linearity in bytes is a per-thread `u128` that cannot overflow by its type.

  - **(1) What the lane was for, and what it became.** The lane's origin is P3's short-route miss. Gate G2+P3 (spec section 16; S3's plan, E11 and section 5.1) asks that the travel estimate be within 15 % at p90 of walked time on static terrain and never optimistic, measured on real commanders, and the test of #187 showed short routes missing it: p90 822 per mille on routes of 4 to 8 cells (the pull request's body). The lane's step 0 (1,080 walks over three seeds) found the cause: the abstract estimate prices the unsmoothed refinement exactly, and on a short route that crosses one cluster border the border's transition node can lie several cells off the line; the smoother cuts that detour for the walker and the estimate still charged it. One off-line border crossing carried 90 % to 99 % of the excess on every band of 32 cells and under, and a cluster corner under 1 % (12 % on the band of 32 to 64 cells). So the corner entrance that G2 had carried to S3 (register S3-11, S3's plan E16, "stays unbuilt unless P3 misses") was measured and not built: P3 missed, but not because of the corner, and `crates/sim/src/pathing/clusters.rs`'s module doc says so and its PLACEHOLDER marker is gone. What the lane became, in the order it was built: part 1 priced a pair whose clusters touch at the route the router serves; part 2 made "nearest" exact (the ranker) and `toward`'s stone the closest legal site over the terrain, over fix passes 2 to 4; the gateway step made a chip's `travel_ms`, what `resolve_refs` binds, `estimate_route`'s answer and the Push's walk one figure, and moved the interface-row bound to the sim's loader; fix pass 5 and 5b built the owner's three answers of (3) and made the walk's quiet defaults typed.
  - **(2) The estimate: "Approve".** Asked whether the travel estimate may be the walk the router serves plus an allowance per extra route, with the estimator's interface changing (items 57 and 61), the owner answered "Approve". As built (`crates/sim/src/pathing/estimate.rs`): a clear query (no fog mask, or one that hides nothing) is priced by `walk_cost`'s own chain, `route_and_abstract`, the router's own function, written into a buffer the scratch owns, and, when the route stops short at `MAX_ROUTE_NODES` (1,024 columns), the rest asked for from where it stops, as the walker asks when it gets there. The cost is the walk's summed step costs; `legs` stays the abstract edge count of the first query; `walk_cost` answers `ServedWalk { cost, partials }`, and `estimate` answers `Estimate { cost, ticks, legs, fogged }`, whose `cost` is the walk's cost, `legs` the first query's abstract edge count and `ticks` is `walk_ticks` of the `ServedWalk`: the cost rounded up to the tick once (`ticks_for_cost`, as item 59 has it), plus `link_ticks` for each partial route. `link_ticks(rows, cap) = (rows - 1) / cap + 1` (integer division, exact by type: `rows` and `cap` are non-zero): the walker banks nothing from one route into the next, so each route rounds up to its own tick (the 1), and the repath queue is served round-robin from a cursor that only moves forward, at most `cap` rows a tick, so a re-ask waits at most `(rows - 1) / cap` ticks after the tick it is made in, however loaded the queue is. `rows` is the world's own unit ceiling (`World::unit_limit`: placement refuses past it and a restore keeps it, refusing a file that holds more), so the allowance is derived once at construction (`World::link_ticks`) and survives a save and resume; a caller that holds only a rules table prices it over `ROOM_LIMIT` (4,095 rows: 256 ticks at the committed cap of 16). On the committed rules the allowance is 20 ticks (1 s) a re-ask at two and at three seats (the pull request's figure for the unit ceiling is 308 rows at two seats and 312 at three; the formula gives 20 for both). **Never optimistic, with its exact conditions as the code documents them** (the module docs' "The error contract"): on static terrain, for a walk under no surcharge, counted from the tick that serves the route, with every later re-ask's wait priced, a walker is never later than `ticks`. A walk served in one route arrives on exactly that tick (`a_walker_arrives_on_the_tick_the_estimate_promised`); a chained walk on it at the latest (`a_chained_walk_arrives_no_later_than_promised`, real commanders through serpentines that need 2, 3 and 5 routes, and `a_re_ask_is_priced_at_the_queues_longest_wait`, which pins the allowance and is red under a mutant that drops it). A surcharged walk (a `move` at `AVOID_KNOWN_THREATS`, an Attack beacon's avoid areas) is not priced and can be later (this condition is not new: the estimate on `main` did not price a surcharge either, though its docs did not say so, and the lane's docs do); no ranked choice is walked under a surcharge (point (5)). **A fogged query keeps the abstract answer** (item 168 (10): the rough estimate under a mask until S4, then priced over the seat's knowledge): under a mask every pair, near or far, takes the abstract search, `cost * 3 / 2` per abstract edge with an unknown endpoint, and its partial routes are bounded by its cost over `1,023` cardinal steps; no production caller sets a mask (the gateway's `RouteAdapter` holds an empty one), and the gap is a PLACEHOLDER in `estimate.rs`'s module docs for the S4 knowledge-store lane. **The API:** `estimate(surface, clusters, scratch, start, goal, fog, speed) -> Result<Option<Estimate>, EstimateError>`; `Ok(None)` is no route, the normal answer (a column off the graph, a route the router could not refine, a walker with no speed); `EstimateError` is `Stalled { partials }` (a chain whose next query did not fall, never read as no route), `PastCost { cost }` and `PastTicks { ticks }` (the sim disagreeing with its own bound, said and never truncated).
